messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Arun was detained while reporting overseas, the abuse unfolded in a room he still cannot picture in a single continuous way. What he can describe are shards: a child crying somewhere beyond a wall, a guard saying a name that now catches in his chest whenever he hears anything similar, the sudden dizziness that came with hunger, fear, and repeated blows. He remembers being forced into situations that left him convinced he had acted against his own values just to survive. Even now, when he tries to tell the story in order, the memory will not come as a coherent account. Parts are blank no matter how hard he tries to reach them, and the pieces he does have feel so extreme that he sometimes says it is like hearing about another man rather than himself.

Back in the United States, Arun returned to journalism but found the ordinary soundscape of his workday had become dangerous. In the newsroom, if a video clip in the background carried the sound of children crying, or if he became lightheaded from missing a meal, or if an interview subject had a name resembling one spoken during his detention, his body reacted before he could think. He would jerk at small noises, scan colleagues’ faces and posture for any sign of threat, and feel a rush of fear, shame, and anger that seemed out of proportion to the moment. Those same moments also pulled at the memory: not in a clear way, but as disjointed flashes and a sick sense of being dropped near something he could neither fully remember nor fully escape.

What frightened Arun almost as much as the memories was what they seemed to say about him. A crying child in a documentary clip could leave him certain that something ruined in him had become visible, that other people could look at him and see exactly what had been done and what he had done to get through it. Hearing a related name could bring back the conviction that there was something fundamentally defective about him. He had come to believe that the event had marked him in a way others would detect immediately, and that belief made every trigger feel more potent; once he started expecting exposure and judgment, he noticed the sounds, names, and bodily sensations everywhere.

Over the months, he began arranging his life around not setting any of this off. He stopped meeting former friends, especially people who had known him before the detention, because being with them made him feel too visible, too aware of the gap between who he had been and who he believed he was now. He ate less and often skipped meals, telling himself he was not hungry, though in practice restriction had become a way to manage feelings he could not otherwise control. He spent long stretches turning over how the detention might have been prevented—what article he should not have pursued, what warning signs he should have noticed, what decision had exposed him. These habits made sense to him as attempts to stay ahead of the next collapse, yet they narrowed his life and deepened his isolation.

The more isolated and underfed he became, the more easily dizziness arrived, and with it another trigger. The more he ruminated about prevention, the more he circled the same inaccessible territory in memory, straining to force a clear account and meeting instead with unreal fragments and gaps. That failure sharpened his vigilance. Because he could not hold the event together, he watched other people more closely, startled more violently at ordinary sounds, and lived with a steady readiness for harm. In those states he judged himself even more harshly: if he was still reacting like this, he thought, it must mean something was deeply wrong with him.

That sense of defectiveness fed directly into his efforts to withdraw. He avoided former social contacts not only to escape questions, but because he was convinced they would see contamination on him. At work he positioned himself near exits, kept conversations brief, and skipped shared lunches, which left him lightheaded by afternoon and more vulnerable to the bodily sensation that reminded him of detention. When he startled in the office, he saw coworkers glance over, and even neutral looks were taken as confirmation that his shame was legible. In that way the threat never stayed confined to his own body; it seemed to live in the room, in other people’s expressions, in names on email chains, in audio clips he could not control.

His attempts to master the past have not brought relief. Deliberately trying to remember has only highlighted what he cannot retrieve, and those gaps themselves have become ominous, as if the missing parts must contain proof of his moral failure. He says the unreality of the memory is one of the worst parts: if it does not feel fully real, he can never be sure it is over. Recently, after jolting at the sound of a child crying during an edit and having to leave the newsroom to steady himself, he realized how much his world had contracted. He is seeking help now because he fears he is losing both his work and any remaining closeness to other people, and because a part of him still hopes it might be possible to remember what happened without feeling that it defines what kind of man he is.
